idiom_name: SafeHandle for OS handles + using/IDisposable; WeakReference<T> for non-owning edges
implementation_notes: .NET has no ownership type for managed objects - the tracing GC holds the graph - so a wrapper that 'owns' another managed object cannot control when it dies. What replaces the classic structure at the unmanaged boundary is System.Runtime.InteropServices.SafeHandle, a framework-provided owning handle that releases through Dispose and, if the caller forgets, through its critical finalizer, with the base class guarding release-once. Managed resources follow IDisposable plus the using statement or declaration, which the compiler rewrites to try/finally and which disposes several resources in reverse declaration order; non-owning edges use System.WeakReference<T> with TryGetTarget. The classic smart-pointer form is still the right answer in one place: adapting a raw OS handle or unmanaged pointer, where a SafeHandle subclass is exactly the owning handle you want.
pitfalls: A SafeHandle must be a reference type (structs cannot derive it) and must not implement its own finalizer - the base class's critical finalizer calls ReleaseHandle exactly once.
TryGetTarget guarantees the target only for the duration of the call: use the out value immediately instead of treating it as a long-lived strong reference.
IDisposable on a type that owns nothing disposable is noise; ownership of managed sub-resources is what makes Dispose meaningful, and cascading to them is still the implementer's job.
The SafeHandle finalizer is a backstop at collection time and costs an extra GC pass; never make it the primary release path.
